note: Texian-held ground is an occupied area until the Republic of Texas is declared on 2 March 1836; after that the Mexican advance is drawn as occupied areas. Lines and areas are approximate reconstructions from campaign maps and the cited accounts.
dataNote: Drawn on the 1835 borders until the end of 1835 and the 1836 borders after; the Republic of Texas counts as a side only from 2 March 1836, and Texian-held ground before that is an occupied area. The 1836 base map draws Texas south only to about the Nueces, so San Patricio's ground is added as part of the Texian area until 27 February 1836.

chapters.title: Gonzales and the Gulf Coast
arrows: Castañeda's dragoons withdraw to Béxar (2–3 October 1835)
Volunteers from Matagorda march on Goliad (6–10 October 1835)
Westover's raid on Fort Lipantitlán (31 October – 4 November 1835)
chapters.text: In late September 1835 Mexican dragoons came to take back a small cannon lent to the settlers of Gonzales. On 2 October about 140 Texian volunteers attacked them and raised a flag reading "Come and Take It", and the dragoons rode back to Béxar. On 10 October volunteers from Matagorda stormed the presidio at Goliad, cutting the Mexican commander Cos off from the coast, and on 3–4 November a small force took Fort Lipantitlán on the Nueces, leaving the Texians in control of the Gulf Coast.

chapters.title: The siege of Béxar
arrows: Austin's army marches from Gonzales on Béxar (12–20 October 1835)
Bowie and Fannin's party moves up to Mission Concepción (27–28 October 1835)
Milam and Johnson storm Béxar (5–9 December 1835)
Cos's paroled army leaves for the Rio Grande (14–20 December 1835)
chapters.text: Stephen F. Austin led the volunteer army from Gonzales to San Antonio de Béxar, where General Cos held the town with about 650 men. On 28 October Texians under James Bowie and James Fannin beat off an attack at Mission Concepción, south of the town, and the army settled into a siege. On 5 December Ben Milam and Frank Johnson led several hundred men into Béxar, fighting house to house for four days. Cos surrendered on 10 December and left with his army, so that no Mexican garrison remained in Texas.

chapters.title: Santa Anna's march and the Alamo
arrows: Santa Anna's army crosses the Rio Grande at Guerrero and marches on Béxar (16–23 February 1836)
The final assault on the Alamo (6 March 1836)
chapters.text: President Santa Anna led an army north through a bitter winter, crossed the Rio Grande at Guerrero on 16 February 1836 and marched up the Camino Real towards Béxar. When his advance guard reached the town on 23 February, its small garrison under William B. Travis and James Bowie fell back into the Alamo mission, and fewer than 100 reinforcements got through to them. On 2 March a convention declared Texas independent. Before dawn on 6 March Mexican columns stormed the Alamo and killed nearly all of its 182 to 257 defenders.

chapters.title: Urrea's coastal campaign and Goliad
arrows: Urrea's column marches from Matamoros to San Patricio (18–27 February 1836)
Mexican dragoons ambush Grant's party at Agua Dulce Creek (2 March 1836)
Urrea advances on Refugio (11–14 March 1836)
Urrea closes on Goliad (16–19 March 1836)
Fannin's retreat from Goliad (19 March 1836)
Urrea takes Victoria (20–21 March 1836)
chapters.text: While Santa Anna besieged the Alamo, General José de Urrea marched up the coast from Matamoros. He surprised Texians at San Patricio on 27 February and at Agua Dulce Creek on 2 March, and in mid-March he defeated William Ward's and Amon King's men at Refugio. James Fannin delayed leaving Goliad until 19 March; Urrea caught his column on the open prairie near Coleto Creek, and Fannin surrendered the next day. Urrea took Victoria on 21 March, and on 27 March, on Santa Anna's orders, about 340 Texian prisoners were shot at Goliad.

chapters.title: The Runaway Scrape
arrows: Houston's army retreats from Gonzales to the Colorado (13–19 March 1836)
Ramírez y Sesma's column follows to the Colorado (14–20 March 1836)
Houston falls back to San Felipe and Groce's Landing (26–31 March 1836)
Gaona's column marches to Bastrop (24 March – 2 April 1836)
Santa Anna and Ramírez y Sesma march on San Felipe (29 March – 7 April 1836)
Urrea advances along the coast to Matagorda (25 March – 13 April 1836)
chapters.text: When news of the Alamo reached Gonzales on 13 March, Sam Houston burned the town and retreated east, and settlers fled ahead of the Mexican columns in what became known as the Runaway Scrape. Houston crossed the Colorado and then fell back to the Brazos, where from 31 March he drilled his army at Groce's Landing. Three Mexican columns followed on roughly parallel roads: Gaona's to Bastrop, Santa Anna's and Ramírez y Sesma's to San Felipe, which they entered on 7 April, and Urrea's along the coast, which took Matagorda on 13 April.

chapters.title: San Jacinto
arrows: Santa Anna crosses the Brazos at Thompson's Ferry (12–13 April 1836)
Santa Anna's dash to Harrisburg and New Washington (14–18 April 1836)
Houston's army marches from Groce's Landing to Harrisburg (13–18 April 1836)
Houston hurries to Lynch's Ferry (19–20 April 1836)
Santa Anna moves to San Jacinto (20 April 1836)
The Texian attack at San Jacinto (21 April 1836)
Urrea advances from Matagorda to Columbia and Brazoria (14–22 April 1836)
chapters.text: Santa Anna crossed the Brazos at Thompson's Ferry and hurried ahead with about 700 men to capture the Texian government, which escaped from Harrisburg and New Washington to Galveston Island. Learning how small and close his force was, Houston marched his 900 men to Lynch's Ferry on Buffalo Bayou, arriving on 20 April. At 4:30 in the afternoon of 21 April the Texians charged the Mexican camp by the San Jacinto River and broke it in about 18 minutes; some 650 Mexican soldiers were killed and 300 captured. Santa Anna was taken the next day, although Urrea's and Filisola's armies still held much of Texas.

battles.name: Battle of Gonzales
battles.casualties: 2 Mexican soldiers killed and 1 wounded; no Texian battle casualties (one man hurt in a fall from his horse)

battles.name: Battle of Goliad (capture of Presidio La Bahía)
battles.casualties: 1–3 Mexican soldiers killed and 3–7 wounded; 1 Texian wounded

battles.name: Battle of Lipantitlán
battles.casualties: 3–5 Mexican soldiers killed and 14–17 wounded; 1 Texian wounded

battles.name: Battle of Concepción
battles.casualties: 14–76 Mexican soldiers killed and 39 wounded; 1 Texian killed and 1 wounded

battles.name: Grass Fight
battles.casualties: 3 Mexican soldiers killed and 14 wounded; 4 Texians wounded

battles.name: Siege of Béxar: the storming of the town
battles.casualties: About 150 Mexican soldiers killed or wounded, and Cos's garrison of about 800 paroled after the surrender; 4–6 Texians killed, Ben Milam among them, and 14–35 wounded

battles.name: Battle of the Alamo
battles.casualties: 182–257 Texian defenders killed; 400–600 Mexican soldiers killed or wounded (the official Mexican report gave 60 killed and 250 wounded)

battles.name: Battle of San Patricio
battles.casualties: 16 Texians killed and 21 captured; 1 Mexican soldier killed and 4 wounded

battles.name: Battle of Agua Dulce Creek
battles.casualties: 12–15 Texians killed, among them James Grant, and 6 captured; 1 Mexican soldier killed

battles.name: Battle of Refugio
battles.casualties: 16 Texians killed in the fighting and about 15 executed, with more captured in the following days; estimates of Mexican killed and wounded range from 150 to 600

battles.name: Battle of Coleto
battles.casualties: About 9–10 Texians killed and 51–67 wounded, the rest of Fannin's 300 or so men captured; about 50 Mexican soldiers killed and 140 wounded

battles.name: Battle of San Jacinto
battles.casualties: About 650 Mexican soldiers killed, 208 wounded and 300 captured; 11 Texians killed and about 30 wounded, Sam Houston among them
